title: Enslaved African Muslims
hookLine: many enslaved Africans brought to the Americas were Muslim, like Omar ibn Said, who wrote in Arabic

lines: A STRANGER IN A CAROLINA JAIL.
cards: Marks on the wall of a small jail in North Carolina. A runaway has been locked up, a stranger who speaks no English anyone can follow. On his cell wall are lines of flowing script in charcoal that nobody can read.
Townspeople come to stare. The man is a scholar from West Africa, and the script is Arabic. He has been carried across an ocean, sold, and has run from a cruel master, and still he writes.
His name is Omar ibn Said, and his story opens a chapter of American history that is easy to miss. Today: enslaved African Muslims.

teach.b: Among the Africans carried across the Atlantic in the slave trade were Muslims.
Some were scholars, teachers and pilgrims, people who could read and write Arabic, had memorized long stretches of the Qur'an, and kept the daily prayers.
They arrived in chains in the Caribbean, Brazil and the American South, and their enslavers often had no idea what the marks on a scrap of paper meant.

teach.h: OMAR IBN SAID OF FUTA TORO.
teach.b: Omar ibn Said came from Futa Toro in West Africa, where he had studied for years. In America he was enslaved, ran away, was jailed, and was then held by a family in North Carolina for the rest of his life.
Years later he wrote a short account of himself, in Arabic. How does he begin?
Not with his own name. After calling on the name of God, he writes out a surah of the Qur'an, al-Mulk, the Dominion.
Its first line, in Pickthall's words: "Blessed is He in Whose hand is the Sovereignty, and, He is Able to do all things."
Consider who is writing: a man owned by another man, opening his life story by saying that the true sovereignty belongs to God.
His enslavers later presented him as a Christian convert, and he did write Christian texts too.
But he kept writing the Qur'an's words, and scholars still debate what he believed in his own heart.

teach.h: IN WHOSE HAND IS THE SOVEREIGNTY.
teach.b: On the Georgia coast, another enslaved Muslim, Bilali Muhammad, left pages of Arabic writing on prayer and law. Men like these wrote Arabic from memory, far from any teacher, and kept the times of prayer.

how: Muslim communities in the Americas, especially African American Muslims, remember enslaved Muslims like Omar ibn Said and Bilali Muhammad in study circles, lectures and museum visits, and some mosques are named in their honor.

practice: Picture the jail wall and the charcoal script, then an old man years later, writing in a language no one around him can read, and the first words he chose.
If you pray, remember Omar and all who were enslaved; if not, keep them company in your mind.
